verses.text: Moab rebelled against Israel after Ahab died.
Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upstairs room in Samaria and was badly hurt. He sent messengers with these instructions: “Go ask Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I'll recover.”
But the angel of the LORD told Elijah the Tishbite, “Go up to meet the king of Samaria's messengers. Ask them, ‘Is there no God in Israel that you're going to ask Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron?
This is what the LORD says: “You won't get up from the bed you're lying on. You'll surely die.”’” So Elijah went.
The messengers returned to Ahaziah, and he asked them, “Why have you come back?”

They answered, “A man met us and told us to go back to you with this message from the LORD: ‘Is there no God in Israel that you sent to consult Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron? Because you did this, you won't get up from the bed you're lying on. You'll surely die.’”
The king asked them, “What did the man who met you and told you this look like?”
They answered, “He was a hairy man and wore a leather belt around his waist.” Ahaziah said, “That's Elijah the Tishbite.”
The king sent a captain with fifty men to get him. The captain found Elijah sitting on top of a hill. “Man of God,” he said, “the king orders you to come down!”
Elijah answered the captain, “If I'm a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” Fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.
The king sent another captain with fifty men. This captain called up, “Man of God, the king orders you to come down at once!”
Elijah answered, “If I'm a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty men.” God's fire came down from heaven and consumed the captain and his fifty men.

The king sent a third captain and his fifty men. This captain climbed the hill, fell to his knees before Elijah, and begged, “Man of God, please spare my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours.
Fire came down from heaven and consumed the other two captains and their men. Please treat my life as precious.”
The angel of the LORD told Elijah, “Go down with him. Don't be afraid of him.” So Elijah got up and went down with him to the king.

Elijah told the king, “This is what the LORD says: ‘You sent messengers to consult Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron. Is there no God in Israel whose word you can ask for? Because you did this, you won't get up from the bed you're lying on. You'll surely die.’”
Ahaziah died, just as the LORD had said through Elijah. Because Ahaziah had no son, Jehoram became king in his place in the second year of the reign of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.
The rest of Ahaziah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
When the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha set out from Gilgal.

Elijah told Elisha, “Please stay here. The LORD has sent me to Bethel.” But Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I won't leave you.” So they went down to Bethel together.
The prophets in training at Bethel came out to Elisha and asked, “Do you know the LORD is taking your master away from you today?” He answered, “Yes, I know. Please be quiet.”

Elijah told him, “Elisha, please stay here. The LORD has sent me to Jericho.” Elisha answered, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I won't leave you.” So they came to Jericho together.
The prophets in training at Jericho came up to Elisha and asked, “Do you know the LORD is taking your master away from you today?” He said, “Yes, I know. Please be quiet.”
Then Elijah said, “Please stay here. The LORD has sent me to the Jordan.” Elisha answered, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I won't leave you.” So the two of them went on.
Fifty men from the company of prophets went and stood facing them at a distance, while Elijah and Elisha stood beside the Jordan.
Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the water with it. The water parted to either side, and both men crossed on dry ground.
After they crossed, Elijah told Elisha, “Tell me what I can do for you before I'm taken away from you.” Elisha asked, “Please let me inherit a double portion of your spirit.”
Elijah said, “You've asked for something hard. If you see me when I'm taken from you, you'll receive it. If you don't see me, you won't.”
As they walked on and talked, a chariot of fire with horses of fire came between them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Elisha saw it and cried, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!” Then he couldn't see Elijah anymore. He grabbed his own clothes and tore them in two.
He picked up the cloak that had fallen from Elijah, went back, and stood on the bank of the Jordan.
He struck the water with Elijah's cloak and asked, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” When he struck the water, it parted to either side, and Elisha crossed.
The company of prophets watching from Jericho saw him and said, “Elijah's spirit rests on Elisha.” They came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him.

They said, “We have fifty strong men here. Please let them go look for your master. The LORD's Spirit may have taken him up and put him on a mountain or in a valley.” Elisha answered, “Don't send them.”
They kept pressing him until he felt too embarrassed to refuse. “Send them,” he said. So they sent fifty men. They searched for three days without finding Elijah.
When they returned to Elisha, who was still in Jericho, he said, “Didn't I tell you not to go?”
The men of the city told Elisha, “My lord, you can see the city is in a good spot. But the water is bad, and the land produces nothing.”
He said, “Bring me a new jar with salt in it.” They brought it to him.
He went to the spring, threw the salt into it, and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘I've healed this water. It will no longer cause death or leave the land barren.’”
The water has remained good to this day, just as Elisha said.
Elisha went up from there to Bethel. As he walked up the road, some youths came out of the city and mocked him. “Go up, baldy!” they shouted. “Go up, baldy!”
He turned, saw them, and cursed them in the LORD's name. Then two female bears came out of the woods and mauled forty-two of the youths.
He went on to Mount Carmel, then returned from there to Samaria.
Jehoram son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in the eighteenth year of King Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah. He ruled for twelve years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, though he didn't go as far as his father and mother. He removed the sacred pillar his father had made for Baal.
Still, he clung to the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into, and he never gave them up.
Mesha king of Moab bred sheep. He supplied the king of Israel with a hundred thousand lambs and the wool from a hundred thousand rams.
After Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
King Jehoram left Samaria and called up all Israel's troops.

He sent word to King Jehoshaphat of Judah: “The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you come with me to fight Moab?” Jehoshaphat replied, “I'll go with you. My people are your people, and my horses are your horses.”
“Which way should we go?” he asked. Jehoram answered, “Through the wilderness of Edom.”
The kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom marched together, taking a roundabout route for seven days. They ran out of water for the troops and the animals traveling with them.
The king of Israel said, “We're in trouble! The LORD has brought these three kings together to hand them over to Moab.”

But Jehoshaphat asked, “Isn't there a prophet of the LORD here so we can ask the LORD what to do?” One of the king of Israel's servants answered, “Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He used to pour water on Elijah's hands.”
Jehoshaphat said, “The LORD's word is with him.” So the kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom went down to see him.

Elisha asked the king of Israel, “What business do I have with you? Go to your father's prophets and your mother's prophets.” The king of Israel answered, “No. The LORD has brought these three kings together to hand them over to Moab.”
Elisha said, “As surely as the LORD of Armies lives, whom I serve, if I didn't respect King Jehoshaphat of Judah, I wouldn't even look at you or give you a hearing.
Now bring me a musician.” While the musician played, the LORD's hand came on Elisha.
He said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Dig trenches all through this valley.’
The LORD says, ‘You won't see wind or rain, but this valley will fill with water, and you, your livestock, and your other animals will drink.
This is easy for the LORD. He'll also hand Moab over to you.
You'll strike every fortified town and every good town. You'll cut down every good tree, plug every spring, and ruin every good field with stones.’”
The next morning, around the time of the offering, water came flowing from the direction of Edom and covered the land.
When the Moabites heard the kings had come to fight them, they assembled everyone old enough to put on armor and took their stand at the border.
They got up early in the morning, and the sun shone on the water. From where they stood, the water looked as red as blood.
“That's blood,” they said. “The kings must have turned on one another and killed each other. Come on, Moab! Let's take the plunder!”
When they reached Israel's camp, the Israelites rose up and attacked the Moabites, who fled from them. The Israelites pressed into Moab, striking them down as they went.

They tore down the towns. Each man threw a stone onto each good field until the fields were covered. They plugged all the springs and chopped down all the good trees. Only the stones of Kir Hareseth were left standing, and the men with slings surrounded it and attacked it.
When the king of Moab saw he was losing the battle, he took seven hundred swordsmen and tried to break through to the king of Edom. They couldn't get through.

Then he took his oldest son, who would have been king after him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the city wall. Great wrath came against Israel, so the Israelites withdrew and went back to their own land.

The wife of a man from the company of prophets cried out to Elisha, “My husband, your servant, is dead. You know he honored the LORD. Now the man he owed money to has come to take my two children as slaves.”
Elisha asked her, “What can I do for you? Tell me what you have in the house.” She answered, “Nothing except a jar of oil.”
He said, “Go borrow empty containers from all your neighbors. Get as many as you can.
Then go inside with your sons and shut the door. Pour oil into all those containers and set each one aside as it fills.”
She left him and shut herself and her sons inside. They brought her the containers, and she poured the oil.
When all the containers were full, she told her son, “Bring me another one.” He said, “There isn't another one.” Then the oil stopped flowing.
She went and told the man of God. He said, “Go sell the oil, pay your debt, and live on what's left, you and your sons.”
One day Elisha went to Shunem. A prominent woman there urged him to stay for a meal. After that, whenever he passed through, he stopped there to eat.
She told her husband, “I can see that this man who keeps coming by is a holy man of God.
Let's make a little room for him on the roof, with a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand. Then he can stay here whenever he comes.”
One day Elisha came and went up to the room to lie down.
He told his servant Gehazi, “Call the woman from Shunem.” Gehazi called her, and she came and stood before him.

Elisha told Gehazi, “Say to her, ‘You've gone to a lot of trouble for us. What can we do for you? Would you like me to speak on your behalf to the king or the army commander?’” She answered, “I live among my own people.”
Elisha asked, “What can we do for her, then?” Gehazi replied, “She has no son, and her husband is old.”
“Call her,” Elisha said. Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway.
Elisha told her, “About this time next year you'll hold a son in your arms.” She said, “No, my lord, man of God. Please don't lie to me.”
But the woman became pregnant and gave birth to a son at that time the next year, just as Elisha had told her.
The boy grew, and one day he went out to his father, who was with the harvesters.
He cried to his father, “My head! My head!” His father told a servant, “Carry him to his mother.”
The servant carried him to his mother. The boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died.
She carried him upstairs, laid him on the man of God's bed, shut the door behind her, and went out.
She called to her husband, “Please send me one of the servants and a donkey so I can hurry to the man of God and come right back.”
“Why are you going today?” he asked. “It isn't the new moon or the Sabbath.” She answered, “It's all right.”
She saddled a donkey and told her servant, “Keep going. Don't slow down for me unless I tell you.”
So she went to see the man of God at Mount Carmel. He saw her coming from a distance and told his servant Gehazi, “Look, it's the woman from Shunem.
Run to meet her and ask, ‘Are you all right? Is your husband all right? Is your child all right?’” She answered, “It's all right.”

When she reached the man of God on the mountain, she grabbed his feet. Gehazi came over to push her away, but the man of God told him, “Leave her alone. She's heartbroken, and the LORD has kept it from me. He hasn't told me what happened.”
Then she said, “Did I ask you for a son, my lord? Didn't I tell you, ‘Don't deceive me’?”
Elisha told Gehazi, “Tuck your cloak into your belt, take my staff, and go. Don't stop to greet anyone you meet, and don't answer anyone who greets you. Lay my staff on the boy's face.”
But the boy's mother said, “As surely as the LORD lives and as surely as you live, I won't leave you.” So Elisha got up and followed her.
Gehazi went on ahead and put the staff on the child's face. There was no sound or response. He went back to meet Elisha and told him, “The boy hasn't woken up.”
When Elisha got to the house, he saw the boy lying dead on his bed.
He went inside, shut the door so they were alone, and prayed to the LORD.
Then he climbed onto the bed and lay over the boy, mouth to mouth, eyes to eyes, and hands to hands. As he stretched himself over him, the boy's body grew warm.
Elisha got up and walked back and forth in the room once. Then he climbed back up and stretched himself over the boy again. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Elisha called Gehazi and said, “Call the woman from Shunem.” He called her, and when she came in, Elisha said, “Pick up your son.”
She came in and fell at his feet, bowing to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.
Elisha returned to Gilgal while there was a famine in the land. The company of prophets was sitting with him, and he told his servant, “Put the big pot on and make some stew for them.”
One of them went into the field to gather herbs. He found a wild vine and gathered a cloakful of wild gourds from it. He came back and sliced them into the pot of stew. Nobody knew what they were.
They served the stew to the men. As they began to eat, they cried out, “Man of God, there's death in the pot!” They couldn't eat it.
Elisha said, “Bring me some flour.” He threw it into the pot and said, “Serve it to the people so they can eat.” There was nothing harmful in the pot anymore.
A man from Baal Shalishah brought the man of God some bread from the first harvest, twenty barley loaves, and fresh heads of grain in his sack. Elisha said, “Give it to the people to eat.”
His servant asked, “How can I put this in front of a hundred people?” Elisha said, “Give it to them to eat. This is what the LORD says: ‘They'll eat and have some left over.’”
So he served them. They ate and had some left over, just as the LORD had said.
Naaman commanded the army of the king of Syria. His master held him in high regard and honored him because the LORD had given Syria victory through him. He was a brave warrior, but he had leprosy.
Some Syrian raiders had taken a young girl captive from Israel, and she served Naaman's wife.
The girl said to her mistress, “If only my master could see the prophet in Samaria! He would heal him of his leprosy.”
Someone went and told his master what the girl from Israel had said.
The king of Syria said, “Go, and I'll send a letter to the king of Israel.” Naaman left, taking ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of clothes.
He took the letter to the king of Israel. It said, “I'm sending my servant Naaman to you with this letter so you can heal him of his leprosy.”

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, able to kill and bring people back to life? Why is this man sending someone to me to cure his leprosy? Look, he's trying to start a fight with me.”
When Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent word to him: “Why did you tear your clothes? Send the man to me, and he'll know there's a prophet in Israel.”
Naaman went with his horses and chariots and stopped at the door of Elisha's house.
Elisha sent a messenger out to tell him, “Go wash yourself in the Jordan seven times. Your skin will be restored, and you'll be clean.”
Naaman stormed off. “I thought he'd come out himself, stand before me, call on the LORD his God, and wave his hand over the affected place to heal me.
Aren't the Abanah and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters in Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean?” He turned and left in a rage.
His servants came up to him and said, “My father, if the prophet had asked you to do something difficult, wouldn't you have done it? So why not do it when all he says is, ‘Wash and be clean’?”
Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, just as the man of God had told him. His skin became like a little child's, and he was clean.
Naaman and all his companions went back to the man of God. Naaman stood before him and said, “Now I know there's no God anywhere on earth except in Israel. Please accept a gift from me.”
Elisha answered, “As surely as the LORD lives, whom I serve, I'll take nothing.” Naaman urged him to take it, but Elisha refused.
Naaman said, “If you won't take it, please let me carry away as much earth as two mules can carry. From now on I won't offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to any god except the LORD.

But may the LORD forgive me for this one thing. When my master goes into Rimmon's temple to worship and leans on my arm, I have to bow there too. When I bow in Rimmon's temple, may the LORD forgive me.”
Elisha said, “Go in peace.” Naaman left and had gone a short distance

when Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said to himself, “My master let this Syrian Naaman go without taking anything he brought. As surely as the LORD lives, I'll run after him and get something from him.”
So Gehazi ran after Naaman. When Naaman saw someone running after him, he got down from his chariot to meet him and asked, “Is everything all right?”

Gehazi said, “Everything's fine. My master sent me to say, ‘Two young men from the company of prophets have just come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothes.’”

Naaman said, “Please take two talents.” He insisted and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, along with two changes of clothes. He gave them to two of his servants, who carried them ahead of Gehazi.
When Gehazi reached the hill, he took the things from the servants and put them away in the house. Then he sent the men away, and they left.
Gehazi went in and stood before his master. “Where have you been, Gehazi?” Elisha asked. “I didn't go anywhere,” he answered.

Elisha said, “Wasn't my heart with you when the man got down from his chariot to meet you? Is this a time to take money or clothes, olive groves or vineyards, sheep or cattle, or male or female servants?
Naaman's leprosy will cling to you and your descendants forever.” Gehazi went out from Elisha's presence with leprosy, his skin white as snow.
The company of prophets told Elisha, “Look, the place where we live and meet with you is too small for us.
Let us go to the Jordan. Each of us can get a beam there, and we can build a place to live.” Elisha said, “Go ahead.”
One of them asked, “Please come with us.” Elisha answered, “I'll go.”
So he went with them. When they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees.
As one man was cutting down a tree, his ax head fell into the water. “Oh, my master!” he cried. “It was borrowed!”
The man of God asked, “Where did it fall?” The man showed him the spot. Elisha cut a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.
“Pick it up,” he said. The man reached out and took it.
The king of Syria was at war with Israel. He consulted his officers and told them where he planned to set up camp.
The man of God sent word to the king of Israel: “Be careful not to pass through that place. The Syrians are coming down there.”
The king of Israel sent men to check the place the man of God had warned him about. This saved him time after time.
The king of Syria was deeply disturbed. He called his officers and asked, “Which of you is on the king of Israel's side? Tell me!”
One of his officers said, “None of us, my lord the king. Elisha, the prophet in Israel, tells the king of Israel the very words you speak in your bedroom.”
The king said, “Find out where he is so I can send men to seize him.” He was told, “He's in Dothan.”
So the king sent horses, chariots, and a large army there. They arrived at night and surrounded the city.
The man of God's servant got up early and went outside. There was an army with horses and chariots all around the city. “Oh, my master!” he cried. “What are we going to do?”
Elisha answered, “Don't be afraid. There are more on our side than on theirs.”
Then Elisha prayed, “LORD, please open his eyes so he can see.” The LORD opened the young man's eyes, and he saw the hillside full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
As the Syrians came down toward him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, “Please strike these people with blindness.” The LORD struck them with blindness, just as Elisha had asked.
Elisha told them, “This isn't the road, and this isn't the city. Follow me, and I'll take you to the man you're looking for.” He led them to Samaria.
When they entered Samaria, Elisha prayed, “LORD, open their eyes so they can see.” The LORD opened their eyes, and they saw that they were right in the middle of Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha, “My father, should I strike them down? Should I?”
Elisha answered, “Don't kill them. Would you kill men you'd taken captive with your sword and bow? Give them bread and water so they can eat and drink, then let them go back to their master.”
The king prepared a great feast for them. After they ate and drank, he sent them back to their master. The Syrian raiding parties stopped coming into the land of Israel.
Later Ben Hadad king of Syria gathered his whole army and laid siege to Samaria.
There was a severe famine in Samaria. The siege went on until a donkey's head sold for eighty pieces of silver and a quarter kab of dove's dung for five pieces of silver.
As the king of Israel walked along the city wall, a woman called out to him, “Help me, my lord the king!”
He said, “If the LORD doesn't help you, where can I find help for you? From the threshing floor or the winepress?”
Then the king asked, “What's wrong?” She answered, “This woman told me, ‘Give us your son to eat today, and tomorrow we'll eat mine.’
So we boiled my son and ate him. The next day I told her, ‘Give us your son so we can eat him,’ but she'd hidden him.”
When the king heard what the woman said, he tore his clothes. He was walking on the wall, and the people could see sackcloth underneath his clothes.
Then he said, “May God punish me severely if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head by the end of today.”

Elisha was sitting at home with the elders when the king sent a messenger ahead of him. Before the messenger arrived, Elisha told the elders, “See how this murderer's son has sent someone to take off my head? When he comes, shut the door and hold it closed. Can't you hear his master's footsteps behind him?”
While Elisha was still talking, the messenger arrived. Then came the words, “This disaster is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?”

Elisha said, “Listen to the LORD's word. This is what the LORD says: ‘About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel and two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel.’”

The officer the king was leaning on said to the man of God, “Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could that happen?” Elisha answered, “You'll see it with your own eyes, but you won't eat any of it.”
Four men with leprosy were at the entrance to the city gate. They asked each other, “Why sit here until we die?
If we go into the city, we'll die there in the famine. If we stay here, we'll die anyway. Let's go surrender to the Syrian army. If they spare us, we'll live. If they kill us, we'll die either way.”
They got up at dusk and headed for the Syrian camp. When they reached the edge of the camp, nobody was there.

The Lord had made the Syrian army hear the sound of chariots and horses, like the approach of a huge army. They said to each other, “The king of Israel must have hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!”
So at dusk they ran for their lives, abandoning their tents, horses, and donkeys and leaving the camp just as it was.

When the four men reached the edge of the camp, they went into a tent and ate and drank. Then they carried away silver, gold, and clothes and hid them. They came back, went into another tent, and took things from there and hid those too.
Then they said to each other, “This isn't right. Today we have good news, and we're keeping it to ourselves. If we wait until morning, we'll be punished. Let's go tell the king's household now.”

They went and called to the city gatekeepers, “We went to the Syrian camp. There was nobody there, not even a voice. The horses and donkeys were still tied up, and the tents were just as they'd left them.”
The gatekeepers called out the news, and it was reported inside the palace.

The king got up in the night and told his servants, “I know what the Syrians are doing. They know we're starving. They've left the camp to hide in the fields. They're thinking, ‘When the people come out of the city, we'll capture them alive and get inside.’”

One of his servants said, “Let some men take five of the horses left in the city. They're as likely to die as the rest of Israel still here, just like all those who have already died. Let's send them to find out.”
They got two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Syrian army. “Go and see,” he said.
They followed the trail as far as the Jordan. The whole road was littered with clothes and equipment the Syrians had thrown away in their hurry. The messengers went back and told the king.
Then the people went out and plundered the Syrian camp. A seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel, just as the LORD had said.
The king had put the officer he leaned on in charge of the gate. The crowd trampled him there, and he died, just as the man of God had said when the king came down to see him.
It happened just as the man of God had told the king: “About this time tomorrow at the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel and a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel.”
That officer had answered the man of God, “Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, could it happen?” Elisha had said, “You'll see it with your own eyes, but you won't eat any of it.”
That's exactly what happened to him. The people trampled him at the gate, and he died.
Elisha told the woman whose son he had brought back to life, “Get up and leave with your household. Stay wherever you can, because the LORD has called for a famine, and it will last seven years.”
The woman did what the man of God said. She left with her household and lived in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
When the seven years were over, she returned from Philistine territory and went to ask the king to give her back her house and land.
The king was talking with Gehazi, the man of God's servant. “Tell me about all the great things Elisha has done,” he said.

Just as Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had brought a dead person back to life, the woman whose son Elisha had restored came to ask for her house and land. Gehazi said, “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha brought back to life.”

The king asked the woman about it, and she told him the story. He assigned an official to her case and said, “Give back everything that belonged to her, including all the produce from her fields from the day she left until now.”
Elisha went to Damascus while Ben Hadad king of Syria was ill. The king was told, “The man of God has come here.”
The king told Hazael, “Take a gift and go meet the man of God. Ask the LORD through him, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’”

Hazael went to meet Elisha, taking gifts of the finest goods in Damascus, as much as forty camels could carry. He stood before him and said, “Your son Ben Hadad king of Syria has sent me to ask, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’”
Elisha told him, “Go tell him, ‘You will surely recover.’ Yet the LORD has shown me that he will surely die.”
Elisha stared steadily at Hazael until Hazael grew uncomfortable. Then the man of God wept.

Hazael asked, “Why are you crying, my lord?” Elisha answered, “I know the terrible things you'll do to Israel. You'll set fire to their strongholds, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little children to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women.”
Hazael said, “How could your servant, a mere dog, do such a thing?” Elisha answered, “The LORD has shown me you'll be king of Syria.”
Hazael left Elisha and went back to his master. Ben Hadad asked, “What did Elisha tell you?” He said, “He told me you'd surely recover.”
The next day Hazael took a thick cloth, soaked it in water, and spread it over the king's face. The king died, and Hazael took his place.
Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat began to rule Judah in the fifth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was still king of Judah.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for eight years.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, just as Ahab's family did, because he'd married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's sight.
Still, the LORD was unwilling to destroy Judah for the sake of his servant David. He had promised that David and his descendants would always have a lamp.
During Jehoram's reign, Edom rebelled against Judah's rule and appointed its own king.
Jehoram crossed over to Zair with all his chariots. The Edomites surrounded him and his chariot commanders, but he rose in the night and struck them. The troops fled to their tents.
Edom has been in rebellion against Judah's rule to this day. Libnah rebelled at the same time.
The rest of Jehoram's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Jehoram died and joined his ancestors and was buried with them in David's City. His son Ahaziah became king in his place.
In the twelfth year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for one year. His mother was Athaliah daughter of Omri king of Israel.
He followed the ways of Ahab's family and did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as they did, because he had married into Ahab's family.
Ahaziah went with Joram son of Ahab to fight Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth Gilead. The Syrians wounded Joram.

King Joram went back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Syrians had inflicted at Ramah while he was fighting King Hazael. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to visit Joram son of Ahab in Jezreel because he was unwell.
Elisha the prophet called one of the prophets in training and told him, “Get ready to travel. Take this flask of oil and go to Ramoth Gilead.
When you get there, find Jehu son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi. Get him to leave the others and take him into an inner room.
Pour the oil on his head and say, ‘This is what the LORD says: “I've anointed you king over Israel.”’ Then open the door and run. Don't wait around.”
So the young prophet went to Ramoth Gilead.
When he arrived, the army commanders were sitting together. He said, “Commander, I have a message for you.” Jehu asked, “Which of us?” He said, “For you, commander.”
Jehu got up and went inside. The prophet poured the oil on his head and told him, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I've anointed you king over the LORD's people Israel.
Strike down the family of your master Ahab. I'll hold Jezebel to account for the blood of my servants the prophets and of all the LORD's servants.
Ahab's entire family will perish. I'll cut off every male in Ahab's family in Israel, whether shut in or free.
I'll make Ahab's family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the family of Baasha son of Ahijah.
Dogs will eat Jezebel on the land at Jezreel, and no one will bury her.’” Then he opened the door and ran.
When Jehu came back out to his master's officers, one of them asked, “Is everything all right? Why did that madman come to see you?” Jehu answered, “You know the man and the sort of things he says.”
They said, “That's a lie. Tell us what he said.” Jehu answered, “He gave me this message from the LORD: ‘I've anointed you king over Israel.’”
They hurried to take off their cloaks and spread them under Jehu at the top of the stairs. Then they blew the trumpet and shouted, “Jehu is king!”
So Jehu son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi plotted against Joram. Joram and all Israel had been defending Ramoth Gilead against Hazael king of Syria.

King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Syrians inflicted while he was fighting Hazael king of Syria. Jehu told the officers, “If you agree with this, don't let anyone get out of the city to take word to Jezreel.”
Jehu got into his chariot and rode to Jezreel, where Joram was still laid up. King Ahaziah of Judah had come down to visit Joram.
The lookout in Jezreel saw Jehu's company approaching from the tower and called out, “I see a group coming.” Joram said, “Send a rider to meet them and ask, ‘Do you come in peace?’”

A rider went to meet Jehu and said, “The king asks, ‘Do you come in peace?’” Jehu answered, “What does peace have to do with you? Get behind me.” The lookout reported, “The messenger reached them, but he isn't coming back.”
Joram sent a second rider. He reached them and said, “The king asks, ‘Do you come in peace?’” Jehu answered, “What does peace have to do with you? Get behind me.”
The lookout reported, “He reached them, but he isn't coming back either. The man drives like Jehu son of Nimshi. He's driving like a madman.”

“Get ready!” Joram said, and his chariot was made ready. King Joram of Israel and King Ahaziah of Judah went out in their own chariots to meet Jehu. They met him on the land that had belonged to Naboth from Jezreel.
When Joram saw Jehu, he asked, “Do you come in peace, Jehu?” Jehu answered, “How can there be peace while your mother Jezebel's prostitution and witchcraft are everywhere?”
Joram pulled his chariot around and fled, shouting to Ahaziah, “It's treason, Ahaziah!”
Jehu drew his bow with all his strength and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow pierced his heart, and he collapsed in his chariot.

Jehu told his officer Bidkar, “Pick him up and throw him onto Naboth's plot of land. Remember how you and I were riding together behind his father Ahab when the LORD pronounced this judgment against him:
‘I saw Naboth's blood and the blood of his sons yesterday,’ says the LORD, ‘and I'll repay you on this very plot of land.’ Now take him and throw him onto the plot, just as the LORD said.”

When King Ahaziah of Judah saw what happened, he escaped by the road to the garden house. Jehu chased him and shouted, “Strike him in his chariot too!” They struck him on the road up to Gur near Ibleam. He fled to Megiddo and died there.
His servants carried him by chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his ancestors in his tomb in David's City.
Ahaziah had become king of Judah in the eleventh year of the reign of Joram son of Ahab.
When Jezebel heard that Jehu had arrived in Jezreel, she put paint around her eyes, arranged her hair, and looked out the window.
As Jehu came through the gate, she called, “Do you come in peace, Zimri, you murderer of your master?”
Jehu looked up at the window and shouted, “Who's on my side? Who?” Two or three eunuchs looked out at him.
“Throw her down!” he said. They threw her down, and her blood splashed on the wall and on the horses. Jehu trampled her underfoot.
He went inside and ate and drank. Then he said, “Take care of this cursed woman and bury her. She's a king's daughter.”
They went to bury her but found only her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.
When they came back and told Jehu, he said, “This is what the LORD said through his servant Elijah the Tishbite: ‘Dogs will eat Jezebel's flesh on the land at Jezreel.
Jezebel's body will be like dung on the ground in the fields of Jezreel, so that no one can say, “This is Jezebel.”’”
Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters and sent them there to the officials of Jezreel, the elders, and the guardians raising Ahab's sons.
The letters said, “Your master's sons are with you, and you have chariots, horses, a fortified city, and weapons. As soon as you get this letter,
pick the best and most qualified of your master's sons, put him on his father's throne, and fight for your master's family.”
They were terrified. “Two kings couldn't stand against him,” they said. “How can we?”

The palace administrator, the city governor, the elders, and the guardians sent this reply to Jehu: “We're your servants and will do whatever you tell us. We won't make anyone king. Do what you think is best.”

Jehu wrote them a second letter: “If you're on my side and will obey me, take the heads of your master's sons and come to me at Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” The seventy princes were in the care of the leading men of the city who were raising them.
When the letter arrived, they took all seventy of the king's sons and killed them. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu in Jezreel.
A messenger told him, “They've brought the heads of the king's sons.” He answered, “Put them in two piles at the city gate and leave them there until morning.”
The next morning Jehu went out and stood before all the people. “You're innocent,” he said. “I plotted against my master and killed him, but who killed all these?
You can be sure that nothing the LORD said about Ahab's family will fail to happen. The LORD has done what he said through his servant Elijah.”
Jehu struck down everyone left from Ahab's house in Jezreel, along with his leading men, close friends, and priests, until no one was left.
Then he set out for Samaria. On the road, at the shepherds' shearing house,
he met relatives of King Ahaziah of Judah. “Who are you?” he asked. They said, “We're Ahaziah's relatives. We're going down to greet the children of the king and the queen.”
“Take them alive,” he ordered. His men seized all forty-two and killed them at the pit by the shearing house. He left none of them alive.

After leaving there, Jehu met Jehonadab son of Rechab coming to meet him. He greeted him and asked, “Are you with me as I'm with you?” Jehonadab said, “I am.” “Then give me your hand,” Jehu replied. Jehonadab did, and Jehu pulled him into the chariot.
“Come with me and see my zeal for the LORD,” Jehu said, and he took Jehonadab along in his chariot.
When Jehu arrived in Samaria, he struck down everyone left of Ahab's family there until he'd destroyed them all, just as the LORD had told Elijah.
Jehu gathered the people and said, “Ahab served Baal a little. Jehu will serve him much more.

Call all Baal's prophets, all his worshipers, and all his priests. Nobody may miss this. I have a great sacrifice to offer Baal. Whoever stays away will die.” Jehu was deceiving them because he meant to destroy Baal's worshipers.
He said, “Set apart a solemn assembly for Baal!” So they announced it.
Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and every one of Baal's worshipers came. They went into Baal's temple and filled it from one end to the other.
He told the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for all Baal's worshipers,” and the keeper brought them out.
Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered Baal's temple. Jehu told Baal's worshipers, “Look around and make sure none of the LORD's servants are here with you. Only Baal's worshipers should be here.”

They went in to make sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had stationed eighty men outside and warned them, “If any of the men I put in your hands gets away, whoever lets him go will pay with his own life.”

As soon as the burnt offering was finished, Jehu ordered the guards and officers, “Go in and kill them. Let no one escape.” They struck the worshipers down with their swords and threw the bodies out. Then they went to the inner shrine of Baal's temple.
They took the sacred pillars out of Baal's temple and burned them.
They tore down Baal's pillar and demolished his temple. They turned the site into a latrine, and it remains one to this day.
That's how Jehu put an end to Baal worship in Israel.
But Jehu held on to the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into, worshiping the gold calves at Bethel and Dan.
The LORD told Jehu, “You did what was right in my eyes and carried out everything I intended for Ahab's family. Your descendants will sit on Israel's throne through the fourth generation.”
Yet Jehu didn't take care to follow the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with his whole heart. He kept on with the sins Jeroboam had led Israel into.
In those days the LORD began cutting away parts of Israel's territory. Hazael attacked Israel all along its borders,
east of the Jordan, throughout Gilead and the territories of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh. That included all Gilead and Bashan, starting at Aroer beside the Arnon valley.
The rest of Jehu's acts, everything he did, and the power he showed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jehu died and joined his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz became king in his place.
Jehu ruled over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years.
When Ahaziah's mother Athaliah saw that her son was dead, she set out to kill all the royal heirs.

But Jehosheba, King Joram's daughter and Ahaziah's sister, took Ahaziah's son Joash away from among the royal sons who were being killed. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom and hid him from Athaliah, so he wasn't killed.
Joash stayed hidden with her in the LORD's house for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.
In the seventh year, Jehoiada sent for the commanders of hundreds of the Carites and the guard. He brought them to the LORD's house, made a covenant with them there, and showed them the king's son.
Then he gave them these orders: “Here's what you must do. A third of those of you coming on duty on the Sabbath will guard the palace.
A third will stand at the Sur Gate, and a third at the gate behind the guard. Together you'll keep watch over the palace and block access.
The two companies going off duty on the Sabbath will stand guard around the king at the LORD's house.
Surround the king, each man with his weapon in hand. Anyone who breaks through your ranks must be killed. Stay with the king wherever he goes.”
The commanders of hundreds did exactly as Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each brought his men to the priest, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty.
The priest gave the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in the LORD's house.
The guards stood with weapons in hand, from one side of the temple to the other, by the altar and the building, with the king inside their ranks.
Jehoiada brought out the king's son, put the crown on him, and gave him the covenant. They made him king and anointed him. Then they clapped and shouted, “Long live the king!”
When Athaliah heard the noise of the guards and the people, she went to the crowd in the LORD's house.

She saw the king standing by the pillar, as was customary, with the commanders and trumpeters beside him. The people of the land were celebrating and blowing trumpets. Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, “Treason! Treason!”

Jehoiada the priest told the commanders in charge of the army, “Take her out between the ranks and kill anyone who follows her with the sword.” The priest had said, “Don't let her be killed in the LORD's house.”
They seized her and took her out by the horses' entrance to the royal palace. She was killed there.
Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD, the king, and the people, that they would be the LORD's people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.

All the people of the land went to Baal's temple and tore it down. They smashed his altars and images to pieces and killed Mattan, Baal's priest, in front of the altars. Jehoiada appointed officers over the LORD's house.

Jehoiada took the commanders, the Carites, the guard, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the LORD's house. They entered the palace through the Guard Gate, and he sat on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. Athaliah had been killed with the sword at the palace.
Jehoash was seven years old when he became king.
Jehoash became king in the seventh year of Jehu's reign. He ruled in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother was Zibiah from Beersheba.
Jehoash did what was right in the LORD's eyes throughout the years when Jehoiada the priest instructed him.
The high places were still there, and the people kept sacrificing and burning incense at them.

Jehoash told the priests, “Collect the money brought as sacred gifts to the LORD's house, including the regular payments, the money assessed for each person, and any money people freely choose to give.
Let each priest take the money from his donors and use it to repair the house wherever damage is found.”
But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash's reign, the priests still hadn't repaired the damage to the house.
King Jehoash called Jehoiada and the other priests and asked, “Why haven't you repaired the house? Stop taking money from your treasurers. Hand it over for the repairs.”
The priests agreed to stop taking money from the people and to give up responsibility for repairing the house.

Jehoiada the priest took a chest, made a hole in its lid, and placed it next to the altar, on the right as you enter the LORD's house. The priests guarding the entrance put all the money people brought to the LORD's house into it.
When there was a lot of money in the chest, the king's scribe and the high priest would come, count the money brought to the LORD's house, and put it in bags.
They weighed out the money and handed it to the supervisors of the work on the LORD's house. The supervisors paid the carpenters and builders working there,
along with the masons and stonecutters. They bought timber and cut stone to repair the damage and paid for everything else needed to repair the LORD's house.
The money brought into the LORD's house wasn't used to make silver cups, wick trimmers, bowls, trumpets, or any gold or silver vessels for it.
It went to the workers, who used it to repair the LORD's house.
They didn't require the men who paid the workers to account for the money they were given, because they handled it honestly.
The money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was kept by the priests and wasn't put into the LORD's house.
Then Hazael king of Syria attacked Gath and captured it. After that, he turned toward Jerusalem.

Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred things dedicated by the earlier kings of Judah, Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, along with the things he himself had dedicated and all the gold in the treasuries of the LORD's house and the palace. He sent it all to Hazael king of Syria, who withdrew from Jerusalem.
The rest of Joash's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
His own servants plotted against him and struck him down at the house of Millo, on the road down to Silla.
His servants Jozacar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer struck him, and he died. He was buried with his ancestors in David's City, and his son Amaziah became king in his place.
In the twenty-third year of the reign of Joash son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for seventeen years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight and followed the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into. He never turned away from them.
The LORD's anger burned against Israel, and he kept handing them over to Hazael king of Syria and to Hazael's son Ben Hadad.
Jehoahaz begged the LORD for help, and the LORD listened to him. He saw how badly the king of Syria was oppressing Israel.
The LORD gave Israel a deliverer, so they escaped Syrian control and lived in their tents again as before.
Even so, they didn't turn from the sins Jeroboam's family had led Israel into. They continued in them, and the Asherah pole still stood in Samaria.
The king of Syria left Jehoahaz only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers. He had destroyed the rest, crushing them like dust at a threshing floor.
The rest of Jehoahaz's acts, everything he did, and the power he showed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jehoahaz died and joined his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. His son Joash became king in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of King Joash's reign over Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for sixteen years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He kept on committing all the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.
The rest of Joash's acts, everything he did, and the power he showed fighting King Amaziah of Judah are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Joash died and joined his ancestors, and Jeroboam took his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
When Elisha became sick with the illness that would kill him, King Joash of Israel came down to see him. He wept over him and cried, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
Elisha told him, “Get a bow and arrows.” So he got a bow and arrows.
Elisha said to the king of Israel, “Put your hand on the bow.” He did, and Elisha laid his hands over the king's hands.

“Open the east window,” Elisha said. The king opened it. “Shoot!” Elisha said, and he shot. Elisha said, “The LORD's arrow of victory! The arrow of victory over Syria! You'll strike the Syrians at Aphek until you've finished them.”
Then he said, “Take the arrows.” The king took them. “Strike the ground,” Elisha said, and the king struck it three times and stopped.
The man of God was angry with him. “You should have struck five or six times,” he said. “Then you'd have defeated Syria completely. Now you'll defeat Syria only three times.”
Elisha died and was buried. Moabite raiding bands used to invade the land at the start of the year.

One day some people were burying a man when they saw a band of raiders. They threw the man's body into Elisha's tomb. As soon as the body touched Elisha's bones, the man came back to life and stood up.
Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel throughout Jehoahaz's reign.
But the LORD was gracious to Israel and had compassion on them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He wouldn't destroy them, and he had not yet driven them from his presence.
Hazael king of Syria died, and his son Ben Hadad became king in his place.
Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben Hadad son of Hazael the towns Ben Hadad had captured from his father Jehoahaz in battle. Joash defeated him three times and recovered the towns of Israel.
In the second year of the reign of Joash son of Joahaz, king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Jehoaddin from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, though he didn't live as his ancestor David had. He followed the example of his father Joash.
The high places remained, and the people kept sacrificing and burning incense there.
As soon as his hold on the kingdom was secure, he executed the servants who had murdered his father the king.

But he spared the murderers' children, following what the LORD commanded in the Book of the Law of Moses: “Parents must not be put to death for what their children did, nor children for what their parents did. Each person will die for their own sin.”
Amaziah struck down ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. He captured Sela in battle and named it Joktheel, the name it bears to this day.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu, the king of Israel. He said, “Come, let's face each other in battle.”

King Jehoash of Israel answered King Amaziah of Judah: “A thistle in Lebanon once sent word to a cedar in Lebanon, ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife.’ Then a wild animal passed by and trampled the thistle.
You defeated Edom, and now you're full of pride. Enjoy your victory and stay home. Why stir up trouble that will bring down both you and Judah?”
Amaziah refused to listen. So King Jehoash of Israel went up, and he and King Amaziah of Judah faced each other at Beth Shemesh in Judah.
Israel defeated Judah, and the men of Judah fled to their own tents.

King Jehoash of Israel captured King Amaziah of Judah, son of Jehoash and grandson of Ahaziah, at Beth Shemesh. Then he went to Jerusalem and tore down four hundred cubits of its wall, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
He took all the gold, silver, and vessels he found in the LORD's house and the palace treasuries. He took hostages too and went back to Samaria.
The rest of Jehoash's acts, the power he showed, and how he fought King Amaziah of Judah are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jehoash died and joined his ancestors. He was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel, and his son Jeroboam became king in his place.
Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived another fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel.
The rest of Amaziah's acts are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
People in Jerusalem plotted against him, so he fled to Lachish. They sent men after him and killed him there.
They brought his body back on horses, and he was buried with his ancestors in Jerusalem, in David's City.
All the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
Azariah rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah. After that, the king died and joined his ancestors.
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for forty-one years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight and kept committing all the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.

He restored Israel's borders from the entrance to Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had said through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath Hepher.
The LORD saw how bitterly everyone in Israel was suffering, slave and free alike. There was no one to help Israel.
The LORD hadn't said he would wipe Israel's name from under heaven. He rescued them through Jeroboam son of Joash.

The rest of Jeroboam's acts, the power he showed, his wars, and how he recovered Damascus and Hamath, which had belonged to Judah, for Israel, are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam died and joined his ancestors, the kings of Israel. His son Zechariah became king in his place.
In the twenty-seventh year of King Jeroboam's reign over Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah became king of Judah.
He was sixteen when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-two years. His mother was Jecoliah from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following the example of his father Amaziah.
The high places remained, and the people kept sacrificing and burning incense there.
The LORD struck the king with leprosy. He had it until the day he died and lived in a separate house. His son Jotham took charge of the palace and governed the people of the land.
The rest of Azariah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Azariah died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in David's City, and his son Jotham became king in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of King Azariah's reign over Judah, Jeroboam's son Zechariah ruled Israel in Samaria for six months.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, as his ancestors had done. He kept committing the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.
Shallum son of Jabesh plotted against him. He struck him down in front of the people, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of Zechariah's acts are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
This fulfilled what the LORD told Jehu: “Your descendants will sit on Israel's throne through the fourth generation.”
Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the thirty-ninth year of King Uzziah's reign over Judah. He ruled in Samaria for one month.
Menahem son of Gadi went up from Tirzah to Samaria. There he struck down Shallum son of Jabesh, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of Shallum's acts and the plot he carried out are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Menahem marched out from Tirzah and attacked Tiphsah, its inhabitants, and the surrounding territory. The city wouldn't open its gates to him, so he attacked and ripped open all its pregnant women.
In the thirty-ninth year of King Azariah's reign over Judah, Menahem son of Gadi became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for ten years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. All his life he kept committing the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.
When Pul king of Assyria came against Israel, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to secure his support and strengthen his hold on the kingdom.
Menahem raised the money by demanding fifty shekels of silver from each wealthy man in Israel, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and didn't stay in the land.
The rest of Menahem's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Menahem died and joined his ancestors, and his son Pekahiah became king in his place.
In the fiftieth year of King Azariah's reign over Judah, Menahem's son Pekahiah became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for two years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He kept committing the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.

His officer Pekah son of Remaliah plotted against him. With Argob, Arieh, and fifty men from Gilead involved, Pekah attacked Pekahiah in the fortified part of the palace in Samaria. He killed him and became king in his place.
The rest of Pekahiah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year of King Azariah's reign over Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for twenty years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight. He kept committing the sins Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into.

During Pekah's reign over Israel, Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria captured Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, including all the land of Naphtali. He took the people captive to Assyria.
In the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah, Hoshea son of Elah plotted against Pekah son of Remaliah. He struck him down, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of Pekah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the second year of the reign of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was Jerusha daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following the example of his father Uzziah.
The high places remained, and the people kept sacrificing and burning incense there. Jotham built the Upper Gate of the LORD's house.
The rest of Jotham's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
In those days the LORD began sending Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.
Jotham died and joined his ancestors and was buried with them in the city of his ancestor David. His son Ahaz became king in his place.
In the seventeenth year of the reign of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. Unlike his ancestor David, he didn't do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel. He even made his son pass through the fire, following the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense at the high places, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.
Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to wage war against Jerusalem. They laid siege to Ahaz but couldn't defeat him.
At that time King Rezin of Syria took Elath back for Syria and drove the people of Judah out. Syrians moved into Elath, and they live there to this day.
Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria with this message: “I am your servant and your son. Come rescue me from the kings of Syria and Israel who are attacking me.”
Ahaz took the silver and gold from the LORD's house and the palace treasuries and sent it to the king of Assyria as a gift.
The king of Assyria listened. He attacked Damascus and captured it, took its people captive to Kir, and killed Rezin.
King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath Pileser king of Assyria. He saw the altar there and sent Urijah the priest a drawing and detailed plans for it.
Urijah the priest built an altar according to the plans King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. He had it ready by the time the king came back.
When the king returned from Damascus and saw the altar, he went up to it and made an offering.
He burned his burnt offering and grain offering, poured out his drink offering, and splashed the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
The bronze altar that stood before the LORD was between Ahaz's altar and the LORD's house. Ahaz moved it from the front of the house to the north side of his own altar.

King Ahaz told Urijah the priest, “Use the large altar for the morning burnt offering, the evening grain offering, my burnt offering and grain offering, and the burnt offerings, grain offerings, and drink offerings of all the people. Splash all the blood from the burnt offerings and sacrifices on it. I'll use the bronze altar when I need to make an inquiry.”
Urijah the priest did everything King Ahaz had ordered.
King Ahaz cut the panels off the stands and removed the basins from them. He also took the Sea down from the bronze oxen underneath it and set it on a stone pavement.
Because of the king of Assyria, he removed the covered passage that had been built for the Sabbath and the king's outer entrance to the LORD's house.
The rest of Ahaz's acts and what he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Ahaz died and joined his ancestors. He was buried with them in David's City, and his son Hezekiah became king in his place.
In the twelfth year of King Ahaz's reign over Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel. He ruled in Samaria for nine years.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, though he didn't go as far as the kings of Israel before him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him. Hoshea became his subject and paid him tribute.

But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea was plotting against him. Hoshea had sent messengers to So king of Egypt and stopped paying the tribute he'd paid every year. So the king of Assyria arrested him and locked him up in prison.
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land and laid siege to Samaria for three years.
In Hoshea's ninth year, the king of Assyria captured Samaria and took the Israelites away to Assyria. He settled them in Halah, along the Habor River in Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes.
This happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of Egypt and rescued them from Pharaoh king of Egypt. They began to worship other gods.
They adopted the customs of the nations the LORD had driven out before them and the practices the kings of Israel had introduced.
In secret the Israelites did things that were wrong against the LORD their God. They built high places in every town, from lonely watchtowers to fortified cities.
They set up sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every leafy tree.
They burned incense at all those high places, just like the nations the LORD had driven out ahead of them. Their wicked actions provoked the LORD to anger.
They served idols even though the LORD had told them, “You must not do this.”

Through every prophet and seer the LORD warned Israel and Judah: “Turn back from your evil ways. Keep my commands and statutes in keeping with the law I gave your ancestors and sent to you through my servants the prophets.”
But they refused to listen. They were as stubborn as their ancestors, who didn't trust the LORD their God.

They rejected his statutes, the covenant he'd made with their ancestors, and his warnings to them. They chased worthless things and became worthless themselves. They imitated the nations around them, though the LORD had told them not to.
They abandoned all the commands of the LORD their God. They cast two calf idols, made an Asherah pole, bowed down to the whole host of heaven, and served Baal.
They made their sons and daughters pass through the fire, practiced divination and spells, and sold themselves to do evil in the LORD's sight, provoking him to anger.
The LORD was so angry with Israel that he removed them from his sight. Only the tribe of Judah remained.
Even Judah didn't keep the commands of the LORD their God. They followed the practices Israel had introduced.
The LORD rejected all Israel's descendants. He afflicted them and handed them over to raiders until he'd thrown them out of his sight.
When he tore Israel away from David's house, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam pulled Israel away from following the LORD and led them into grave sin.
The Israelites kept committing all the sins Jeroboam had committed. They didn't turn from them
until the LORD removed Israel from his sight, just as he'd warned through all his servants the prophets. Israel was taken from its own land into Assyria, where the people remain to this day.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the towns of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took over Samaria and lived in its towns.
When they first settled there, they didn't honor the LORD. So the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions killed some of them.

The king of Assyria was told, “The people you moved into the towns of Samaria don't know the law of the god of that land. He's sent lions among them, and the lions are killing them because they don't know his law.”
The king of Assyria ordered, “Send back one of the priests you took from there. Let him live there and teach the people the law of the god of the land.”
So one of the priests who had been taken from Samaria came back and lived in Bethel. He taught them how to honor the LORD.
Still, each nation made its own gods and set them in the shrines the Samaritans had built at the high places in the towns where they now lived.
The people from Babylon made Succoth Benoth, those from Cuth made Nergal, and those from Hamath made Ashima.
The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the people from Sepharvaim burned their children in the fire for their gods Adrammelech and Anammelech.
They honored the LORD too and appointed people from among themselves to serve as priests who sacrificed for them at the shrines on the high places.
They honored the LORD while serving their own gods, following the customs of the nations from which they'd been taken.
To this day they still follow their old customs. They don't truly honor the LORD or obey the statutes, rulings, law, and commands the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.
The LORD had made a covenant with them and commanded them, “Don't fear other gods or bow down to them, serve them, or offer sacrifices to them.
Honor the LORD, who brought you out of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm. Bow down to him and offer your sacrifices to him.
Always be careful to follow the statutes, rulings, law, and commands he wrote for you. Don't fear other gods.
Don't forget the covenant I made with you, and don't fear other gods.
Honor the LORD your God, and he'll rescue you from all your enemies.”
They refused to listen and kept following their old customs.
These nations honored the LORD while serving their carved images. Their children and grandchildren did the same. To this day they do what their ancestors did.
In the third year of the reign of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Abi daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes, following the example of his ancestor David.

He removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah pole. He also broke up the bronze snake Moses had made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it. He called it Nehushtan.
He trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. There was no one like him among all the kings of Judah, before him or after him.
He held on to the LORD and never turned away from following him. He kept the commands the LORD had given Moses.
The LORD was with him, and he succeeded wherever he went. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.
He struck the Philistines as far as Gaza and its surrounding territory, from the watchtowers to the fortified cities.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah's reign, the seventh year of the reign of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked Samaria and laid siege to it.
After three years the Assyrians captured it. Samaria fell in Hezekiah's sixth year, which was the ninth year of King Hoshea's reign over Israel.
The king of Assyria took Israel into exile in Assyria and settled them in Halah, along the Habor River in Gozan, and in the towns of the Medes.
This happened because they had disobeyed the LORD their God and broken his covenant. They refused to listen to or carry out what Moses, the LORD's servant, had commanded.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah's reign, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish: “I've offended you. Withdraw, and I'll pay whatever you demand.” The king of Assyria demanded three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold from him.
Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in the LORD's house and the palace treasuries.
At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of the LORD's temple and from the doorposts he had covered with gold. He gave it to the king of Assyria.

The king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh from Lachish with a large army to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. When they reached Jerusalem, they stood beside the channel from the Upper Pool, on the road to the cloth washer's field.
They called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who ran the palace household, came out to them along with Shebnah the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, who kept the records.
Rabshakeh told them, “Give Hezekiah this message from the great king, the king of Assyria: ‘What are you relying on?
You say you have plans and strength for war, but that's empty talk. Who do you trust so much that you've rebelled against me?
You're leaning on Egypt, that splintered reed of a walking stick. If you lean on it, it will pierce your hand. That's what Pharaoh king of Egypt does to anyone who relies on him.
You might tell me, “We trust in the LORD our God.” Isn't that the god whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed when he told Judah and Jerusalem, “You must worship at this altar in Jerusalem”?
Come on, make a deal with my master, the king of Assyria. I'll give you two thousand horses if you can find enough riders for them.
How can you turn back even one of my master's lowest officers when you're relying on Egypt for chariots and horsemen?
Have I come to destroy this place without the LORD's approval? The LORD himself told me, “Go up against this land and destroy it.”’”
Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebnah, and Joah told Rabshakeh, “Please speak to us in Aramaic. We understand it. Don't speak to us in the language of Judah where the people on the wall can hear.”
Rabshakeh replied, “Did my master send me to speak only to you and your master? The men sitting on the wall will have to eat their own dung and drink their own urine right along with you.”
Then Rabshakeh stood and shouted in the language of Judah, “Listen to the message of the great king, the king of Assyria.
This is what the king says: ‘Don't let Hezekiah deceive you. He can't rescue you from my hand.
Don't let Hezekiah talk you into trusting the LORD by saying, “The LORD will surely rescue us. This city won't fall into the hands of the king of Assyria.”
Don't listen to Hezekiah. The king of Assyria says, “Make peace with me and come out to me. Each of you will eat from your own vine and fig tree and drink from your own cistern,

until I come and take you to a land like your own, a land of grain and new wine, bread and vineyards, olive trees and honey. Then you'll live instead of dying.” Don't listen when Hezekiah tries to persuade you by saying, “The LORD will rescue us.”
Has any nation's god ever rescued its land from the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?
Which of all the gods of these lands has rescued their country from my hand? Why should the LORD be able to rescue Jerusalem from my hand?’”
The people stayed silent and didn't say a word, because the king had ordered them, “Don't answer him.”
Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the record keeper, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him what Rabshakeh had said.
When King Hezekiah heard the report, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went into the LORD's house.
He sent the palace administrator Eliakim, Shebna the scribe, and the senior priests to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz. They were all dressed in sackcloth.
They told Isaiah, “Hezekiah says, ‘Today is a day of trouble, rebuke, and disgrace. It's like a child is ready to be born, but the mother has no strength to give birth.

Maybe the LORD your God will hear what Rabshakeh said when his master, the king of Assyria, sent him to defy the living God. Maybe the LORD will rebuke him for those words. So please pray for the few of us who are left.’”
King Hezekiah's servants came to Isaiah with this message.
Isaiah told them, “Tell your master, ‘This is what the LORD says: “Don't be afraid of the words you heard from the servants of the king of Assyria. They have insulted me.
I'll put a spirit in him so he hears a report and goes back to his own country. I'll cause him to fall by the sword there.”’”
Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, so he went back and found him fighting against Libnah.
Then the king heard that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia had come out to fight him. He sent messengers to Hezekiah again.
“Tell Hezekiah king of Judah, ‘Don't let the God you trust deceive you by saying Jerusalem won't be handed over to the king of Assyria.
You've heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands they've completely destroyed. Do you think you'll escape?
Did the gods of the nations my ancestors destroyed rescue Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, or the people of Eden in Telassar?
Where are the kings of Hamath, Arpad, the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’”
Hezekiah took the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to the LORD's house and spread the letter out before the LORD.
Hezekiah prayed, “LORD, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God over every kingdom on earth. You made heaven and earth.
Listen, LORD, and hear. Open your eyes, LORD, and see. Hear what Sennacherib wrote to defy the living God.
It's true, LORD, that the kings of Assyria have devastated the nations and their lands.
They threw those nations' gods into the fire. They were only wood and stone shaped by human hands, so the Assyrians could destroy them.
Now, LORD our God, please save us from his hand so every kingdom on earth will know that you alone, LORD, are God.”
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah: “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I heard your prayer to me about Sennacherib king of Assyria.’
This is what the LORD says about him: ‘The virgin daughter of Zion despises you and laughs at you. The daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head at you.
Who do you think you've defied and insulted? Against whom did you raise your voice and lift your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!

You sent your messengers to defy the Lord. You said, “With all my chariots I've climbed the highest mountains, deep into Lebanon. I'll cut down its tallest cedars and finest cypress trees. I'll reach its most distant shelter and its richest forest.
I've dug wells and drunk water in foreign lands. I'll dry up all Egypt's rivers with the soles of my feet.”
Haven't you heard? I planned this long ago. I laid it out in ancient times, and now I've brought it about. I let you turn fortified cities into heaps of rubble.
That's why their people had no strength. They were frightened and confused, like grass in a field, like tender green plants, like grass on rooftops or grain scorched before it can grow.
I know when you sit down, when you go out, and when you come in. I know how you've raged against me.
Your rage and your arrogance have reached my ears. So I'll put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth and turn you back by the road you came.’
