“This will be the sign for you, Hezekiah. This year you'll eat what grows by itself. Next year you'll eat what grows from that. In the third year, sow and harvest, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.
The survivors from Judah will put down roots again and bear fruit.
A remnant will come out of Jerusalem, and survivors will come out of Mount Zion. The LORD's zeal will make it happen.
“So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: ‘He won't enter this city or shoot an arrow into it. He won't come up to it with a shield or build a siege ramp against it.
He'll go back the way he came. He won't enter this city,’ says the LORD.
‘I'll defend this city and save it for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.’”
That night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the Assyrian camp. When people got up in the morning, there were dead bodies everywhere.
Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and went back home to Nineveh, where he stayed.

While he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esar Haddon became king in his place.

Around that time Hezekiah became sick and was about to die. Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, came to him and said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘Put your affairs in order. You're going to die. You won't recover.’”
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD.
“Please remember, LORD, how faithfully I've walked before you, with my whole heart, and how I've done what is good in your sight.” Then Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Before Isaiah had reached the middle of the city, the LORD spoke to him again:

“Go back and tell Hezekiah, the ruler of my people, ‘This is what the LORD, the God of your ancestor David, says: “I've heard your prayer and seen your tears. I'll heal you. On the third day you'll go up to the LORD's house.
I'll add fifteen years to your life and rescue you and this city from the king of Assyria. I'll defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.”’”
Isaiah said, “Bring a cake of figs.” They brought it and laid it on the boil, and Hezekiah recovered.
Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “What sign will show that the LORD will heal me and that I'll go up to his house on the third day?”
Isaiah said, “The LORD will give you a sign that he'll do what he promised. Should the shadow go forward ten steps or go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah answered, “It's easy for the shadow to go forward ten steps. Let it go back ten steps instead.”
Isaiah the prophet called out to the LORD, and the LORD moved the shadow back ten steps on Ahaz's sundial.
Around that time Berodach Baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, heard Hezekiah had been sick and sent him letters and a gift.

Hezekiah welcomed the messengers and showed them everything in his storehouses: silver, gold, spices, fine oil, his armory, and all his treasures. There was nothing in his palace or in his whole kingdom that he didn't show them.
Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and asked, “What did those men say? Where did they come from?” Hezekiah said, “They came from a distant country, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What did they see in your palace?” Hezekiah answered, “They saw everything. There wasn't a single treasure I didn't show them.”
Then Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Listen to the LORD's word.
‘The days are coming when everything in your palace and everything your ancestors stored up to this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left,’ says the LORD.
‘Some of your own descendants will be taken away and made eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.’”
Hezekiah told Isaiah, “The word of the LORD you've spoken is good.” He added, “Isn't it good if there'll be peace and security in my lifetime?”
The rest of Hezekiah's acts, all the power he showed, and how he built the pool and the channel to bring water into the city are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Hezekiah died and joined his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.
Manasseh was twelve when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for fifty-five years. His mother was Hephzibah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following the detestable practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before Israel.

He rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed. He put up altars for Baal and made an Asherah pole as King Ahab of Israel had done. He bowed down to the whole host of heaven and served them.
He built altars in the LORD's house, even though the LORD had said, “I'll put my name in Jerusalem.”
He built altars for the whole host of heaven in both courtyards of the LORD's house.
He made his son pass through the fire, practiced sorcery and spells, and consulted mediums and spiritists. He did much that was evil in the LORD's sight and provoked him to anger.

He put the carved Asherah image he'd made inside the house the LORD had spoken about to David and his son Solomon: “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I've chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I'll put my name forever.
I'll never again make Israel wander away from the land I gave their ancestors, if they'll carefully do all I've commanded and follow all the law my servant Moses gave them.”
But the people refused to listen. Manasseh led them into worse evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed ahead of Israel.
The LORD spoke through his servants the prophets:
“Manasseh king of Judah has done these detestable things. He's acted more wickedly than the Amorites who came before him, and his idols have led Judah into sin.
So this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I'll bring such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that both ears of everyone who hears about it will ring.
I'll stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line I used on Samaria and the plumb line I used on Ahab's family. I'll wipe Jerusalem clean like someone wiping a dish, then turn it upside down.
I'll cast away the rest of my inheritance and hand them over to their enemies. Their enemies will seize them and take everything they have.
They've done what is evil in my sight and provoked me to anger from the day their ancestors came out of Egypt right up to today.’”
Manasseh also shed so much innocent blood that he filled Jerusalem with it from one end to the other. This was on top of the sin he led Judah into by doing what was evil in the LORD's sight.
The rest of Manasseh's acts, everything he did, and the sin he committed are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Manasseh died and joined his ancestors. He was buried in the garden of his own palace, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for two years. His mother was Meshullemeth daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed all his father's ways. He served the same idols his father had served and bowed down to them.
He abandoned the LORD, the God of his ancestors, and refused to follow the LORD's ways.
Amon's own servants plotted against him and killed him in his palace.
The people of the land killed everyone who had plotted against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah king in his place.
The rest of Amon's acts and what he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother was Jedidah daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath.
He did what was right in the LORD's eyes and followed all the ways of his ancestor David without turning to the right or the left.
In the eighteenth year of his reign, King Josiah sent Shaphan the scribe, son of Azaliah and grandson of Meshullam, to the LORD's house with these instructions:
“Go to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count the money brought into the LORD's house, the money the guards at the entrance have collected from the people.
Have them hand it to the supervisors working on the LORD's house. Let the supervisors pay the workers who are repairing the damage to the house,
including the carpenters, builders, and masons, and let them buy the timber and cut stone they need for the repairs.
Don't require them to account for the money they receive, because they handle it honestly.”
Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan the scribe, “I've found the Book of the Law in the LORD's house.” He handed the book to Shaphan, and Shaphan read it.
Shaphan the scribe went back to the king and reported, “Your servants emptied out the money found in the house and handed it to the men supervising the work on the LORD's house.”
Then Shaphan told the king, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book.” Shaphan read it to the king.
When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.
The king gave instructions to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king's servant:

“Go ask the LORD on behalf of me, the people, and all Judah about the words in this book that was found. The LORD's anger burns fiercely against us because our ancestors didn't listen to the words of this book and didn't do everything written there for us.”

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to speak with Huldah the prophet. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah and grandson of Harhas, who kept the wardrobe. She lived in the Second Quarter of Jerusalem.
Huldah said to them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Tell the man who sent you to me,
“This is what the LORD says: I'll bring disaster on this place and its people. Everything written in the book the king of Judah has read will happen.
They abandoned me and burned incense to other gods, provoking me to anger with all the things they made. My anger will burn against this place, and it won't be put out.”
But tell the king of Judah who sent you to ask the LORD, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the words you've heard:

Your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I said against this place and its people, that they would become a ruin and a curse. You tore your clothes and wept before me. I have heard you, says the LORD.
So I'll gather you to your ancestors, and you'll go to your grave in peace. You won't see the disaster I'm going to bring on this place.”’” They took her answer back to the king.
The king sent for all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem, and they gathered before him.

He went up to the LORD's house with the people of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests and prophets, and everyone from the least to the greatest. He read aloud all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the LORD's house.

The king stood beside the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD to follow him and keep his commands, testimonies, and statutes with all his heart and soul. He pledged to carry out the words of the covenant written in the book, and all the people joined in the covenant.

The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests next in rank, and the guards at the entrance to take out of the LORD's temple all the articles made for Baal, Asherah, and the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields by the Kidron and took their ashes to Bethel.

He removed the priests the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense at the high places in Judah's towns and around Jerusalem, including those who burned incense to Baal, the sun, the moon, the planets, and the whole host of heaven.

He took the Asherah pole out of the LORD's house and brought it outside Jerusalem to the Kidron stream. He burned it there, crushed it to dust, and scattered the dust on the graves of ordinary people.
He tore down the quarters of the male shrine prostitutes in the LORD's house, where women wove cloth hangings for Asherah.

He brought the priests out of all the towns of Judah and made the high places where they burned incense unfit for worship, from Geba to Beersheba. He tore down the shrines at the gates, including those at the entrance to the gate of Joshua the city governor, on the left as you enter the city.
The priests who had served at the high places didn't serve at the LORD's altar in Jerusalem, though they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests.
Josiah defiled Topheth in the Valley of Ben Hinnom so no one could make a son or daughter pass through the fire for Molech.

He removed the horses the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance to the LORD's house, beside the room of Nathan Melech, an official in the courtyard. He burned up the chariots dedicated to the sun.

The king tore down the altars the kings of Judah had built on the roof above Ahaz's upper room and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of the LORD's house. He crushed them and threw the dust into the Kidron stream.

The king defiled the high places east of Jerusalem on the south side of the Mount of Corruption. King Solomon of Israel had built them for Ashtoreth, the detestable goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and Milcom, the detestable god of the Ammonites.
Josiah smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and covered those places with human bones.
He also tore down the altar at Bethel and the high place built by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel into sin. He burned the high place, crushed it to dust, and burned the Asherah pole.

When Josiah turned and saw the tombs on the hillside, he had the bones taken out and burned on the altar to make it unfit for worship. This fulfilled the LORD's word that the man of God had proclaimed.
Josiah asked, “What's that monument I see?” The townspeople answered, “It's the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and foretold what you've just done to the altar at Bethel.”
“Leave him alone,” Josiah said. “Nobody move his bones.” So they left his bones and those of the prophet from Samaria undisturbed.
Josiah removed all the shrines at the high places in the towns of Samaria that the kings of Israel had built to provoke the LORD to anger. He did to them what he'd done at Bethel.
He killed all the priests of those high places on their altars and burned human bones there. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
The king told all the people, “Celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, as written in this Book of the Covenant.”
A Passover like this hadn't been celebrated since the days when judges led Israel, or throughout the days of the kings of Israel and Judah.
But in King Josiah's eighteenth year, this Passover was celebrated to the LORD in Jerusalem.

Josiah also got rid of the mediums and spiritists, household gods, idols, and all the detestable things found in Judah and Jerusalem. He did this to carry out the law written in the book Hilkiah the priest found in the LORD's house.
No king before Josiah turned to the LORD as he did, with all his heart, soul, and strength according to the whole law of Moses. No king like him came after him either.
Still, the LORD didn't turn away from his fierce anger against Judah because Manasseh had provoked him so deeply.
The LORD said, “I'll remove Judah from my sight as I removed Israel. I'll reject Jerusalem, the city I chose, and the house where I said, ‘My name will be there.’”
The rest of Josiah's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

During Josiah's reign, Pharaoh Necoh king of Egypt went up toward the Euphrates to confront the king of Assyria. King Josiah went out to meet him in battle, and Pharaoh Necoh killed him at Megiddo when they met.

Josiah's servants carried his body from Megiddo to Jerusalem in a chariot and buried him in his tomb. The people of the land took his son Jehoahaz, anointed him, and made him king in his father's place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he became king and ruled in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following the ways of his ancestors.
Pharaoh Necoh put him in chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath so he couldn't rule in Jerusalem. He made the land pay a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.
Pharaoh Necoh made Josiah's son Eliakim king in his father's place and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz away to Egypt, where he died.
Jehoiakim gave Pharaoh the silver and gold. To pay what Pharaoh demanded, he taxed the people of the land, taking silver and gold from each person according to their assessment.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Zebidah daughter of Pedaiah from Rumah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following the ways of his ancestors.
During Jehoiakim's reign, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon invaded. Jehoiakim served him for three years, then turned against him and rebelled.
The LORD sent Babylonian, Syrian, Moabite, and Ammonite raiding parties against Jehoiakim. He sent them to destroy Judah, just as he'd said through his servants the prophets.
This happened at the LORD's command to remove Judah from his sight because of all the sins Manasseh had committed.
It happened also because Manasseh had shed innocent blood. He'd filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the LORD was unwilling to forgive it.
The rest of Jehoiakim's acts and everything he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Jehoiakim died and joined his ancestors. His son Jehoiachin became king in his place.
The king of Egypt didn't venture outside his land again. The king of Babylon had taken everything that belonged to him from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Nehushta daughter of Elnathan from Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, following everything his father had done.
At that time the troops of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem and laid siege to the city.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon arrived while his troops were besieging it.
Jehoiachin king of Judah went out to the king of Babylon with his mother, his servants, his officials, and his officers. The king of Babylon took him captive in the eighth year of his own reign.

The king of Babylon carried away all the treasures of the LORD's house and the royal palace. He cut up the gold vessels Solomon king of Israel had made for the LORD's temple, just as the LORD had said.

He took Jerusalem into exile, including all its officials and fighting men, ten thousand captives in all, along with the craftsmen and metalworkers. Only the poorest people of the land were left behind.
He took Jehoiachin into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon, along with the king's mother, wives, officers, and the leading men of the land.
The king of Babylon also took seven thousand fighting men and a thousand craftsmen and metalworkers captive to Babylon. They were all strong and fit for war.
The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king in his place and changed his name to Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the LORD's sight, doing just what Jehoiakim had done.
All this happened to Jerusalem and Judah because of the LORD's anger, until he cast them out of his presence. Then Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

On the tenth day of the tenth month of Zedekiah's ninth year as king, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. They camped outside it and built siege works all around it.
The city remained under siege until King Zedekiah's eleventh year.
By the ninth day of the fourth month, famine in the city was so severe that there was no bread left for the people.

A breach was made in the city wall. All the soldiers fled at night through the gate between the two walls by the king's garden. The Babylonian army still surrounded the city, and the king fled toward the Arabah.
The Babylonian army chased the king and caught him in the plains of Jericho. All his troops scattered, leaving him behind.
They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where they passed sentence on him.
They killed Zedekiah's sons in front of him. Then they put out his eyes, bound him in chains, and took him to Babylon.
On the seventh day of the fifth month, in the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard and an official of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the LORD's house, the royal palace, and the houses of Jerusalem. He set fire to every important building.
The whole Babylonian army under the captain of the guard tore down the walls around Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan took into exile the people still in the city, those who had surrendered to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the population.
But the captain of the guard left some of the poorest people in the land to work the vineyards and fields.
The Babylonians broke apart the bronze pillars, the stands, and the bronze Sea in the LORD's house. They carried the bronze pieces back to Babylon.
They took the pots, shovels, wick trimmers, spoons, and all the bronze articles used in temple service.
The captain of the guard also took the firepans and bowls, along with everything made of gold or silver.
The bronze in the two pillars, the Sea, and the stands Solomon made for the LORD's house was never weighed.

One pillar was eighteen cubits tall and had a bronze capital three cubits high. Latticework and pomegranates surrounded the capital, all of bronze. The second pillar had the same design and latticework.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the priest next in rank, and the three guards at the entrance to the temple.

From the city he took an officer in charge of the soldiers, five of the king's advisers found there, the army commander's scribe who called up the people of the land, and sixty men of the land found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, took them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
The king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah was taken captive out of its land.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan governor over the people he'd left in Judah.

When the army commanders and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah, they went to him at Mizpah. They included Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth from Netophah, and Jaazaniah son of the Maacathite, with their men.
Gedaliah gave them and their men his word: “Don't be afraid of the Babylonian officials. Stay in the land and serve the king of Babylon, and things will go well for you.”

But in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and grandson of Elishama, a member of the royal family, came with ten men. They killed Gedaliah and the people of Judah and Babylon who were with him at Mizpah.
Then all the people, from the least to the greatest, and the army commanders left for Egypt because they were afraid of the Babylonians.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the first year of Evil Merodach's reign as king of Babylon, he released Jehoiachin from prison. It was the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month.
He spoke kindly to Jehoiachin and gave him a seat of honor above the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
Jehoiachin took off his prison clothes and ate regularly at the king's table for the rest of his life.
The king gave him a regular allowance, a portion every day as long as he lived.
